verse.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope,
to Timothy, a true child in faith: Grace, mercy, peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
As I urged you when I was setting out for Macedonia, stay on in Ephesus so that you may command certain people not to teach anything different
verse.note: The Greek sentence begins ‘Just as I urged you to stay on in Ephesus…’ and breaks off without a main clause. Like most translations, this one completes the thought by turning the urging into a direct instruction. Some instead take the sentence to be left hanging, with the conclusion (‘so I urge you now’) understood.

verse.text: or to occupy themselves with myths and endless genealogies. These give rise to speculations rather than to God's stewardship, which is in faith.

note.traditional: godly edifying (KJV, from a different reading); God's work; the divine training

verse.note: The word means the management of a household or the task of a household manager, and by extension an arrangement or plan. Here it may mean the responsibility God has entrusted to his servants, carried out in faith, or God's own ordering of salvation, received by faith. The rendering keeps the household image, which recurs in this letter, but both readings have strong support. A few manuscripts read ‘edification’ instead.

verse.text: But the goal of the command is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and a sincere faith.
Some have strayed from these and turned aside to empty talk,
wanting to be teachers of the law, though they understand neither what they are saying nor the things they so confidently assert.
Now we know that the law is good if one uses it lawfully,

knowing this: law is not laid down for a righteous person but for the lawless and rebellious, the ungodly and sinners, the unholy and profane, those who strike their fathers and those who strike their mothers, murderers,

note.term: those who strike their fathers and those who strike their mothers
note.traditional: murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers

verse.note: These two rare words can mean someone who kills a parent or someone who beats one; in earlier Greek the sense of assault is well attested. Most English versions have ‘kill’, but ‘murderers’ follows as a separate item. The list also appears to track the Ten Commandments, where honoring parents precedes the ban on murder (compare Exodus 21:15 on striking a parent). ‘Strike’ covers both senses; the narrower meaning ‘parricide’ remains possible.

verse.text: the sexually immoral, men who lie with males, enslavers, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is opposed to healthy teaching,

note.traditional: sodomites; homosexuals; men who practice homosexuality

verse.note: This compound of ‘male’ and ‘bed’ is not found before Paul (also 1 Corinthians 6:9) and was almost certainly formed from the Greek wording of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13. Most scholars take it to refer to men who have sexual intercourse with males. Some argue for a narrower reference to exploitative relations such as pederasty or prostitution, but the evidence is thin because the word is so rare. The rendering keeps the echo of Leviticus and avoids modern categories of orientation, which the word does not express.

The word refers to someone who seizes free people, or steals other people's slaves, in order to sell them. Kidnapping for sale was a recognized crime in both Greek and Roman law and is condemned in Exodus 21:16. The word does not by itself condemn the legal ownership of slaves, which was a normal institution of the time.

The Greek word is the ordinary verb for being in good health, and the letters to Timothy and Titus repeatedly contrast ‘healthy’ teaching with teaching described as diseased. ‘Sound’ once conveyed this but is now a faded metaphor. Philosophers of the period used the same image for right thinking, so the sense ‘correct, wholesome’ is not in dispute.

verse.text: according to the good news of the glory of the blessed God, with which I was entrusted.
verse.note: The Greek was an everyday word for the announcement of good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations. ‘Gospel’ has become a purely religious term or the name of a kind of book. Many modern translations already alternate between the two renderings.

verse.text: I am grateful to the one who has strengthened me, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he considered me faithful and appointed me to service,
though I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and a man of insolent violence. But I was shown mercy, because I acted in ignorance, in unbelief,
and the grace of our Lord overflowed beyond measure, together with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.
The saying is trustworthy and worthy of full acceptance: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.
verse.note: The same adjective is rendered ‘faithful’ in verse 12, where it describes a person. Applied to a statement it means reliable, and ‘a faithful saying’ is no longer natural English. The Greek plays on one word-family throughout this passage: Paul is ‘entrusted’ (v. 11), counted ‘faithful’ (v. 12), once acted in ‘unbelief’ (v. 13), and cites a ‘trustworthy’ saying for those who will ‘believe’ (v. 16).

verse.text: But for this reason I was shown mercy: so that in me, the foremost, Christ Jesus might display all his patience, as a pattern for those who were going to believe in him for eternal life.
Now to the King of the ages, imperishable, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory to the ages of the ages. Amen.

note.term: to the ages of the ages

verse.note: The Greek idiom, modelled on Hebrew, means ‘for all time’, and ‘forever and ever’ is an accurate paraphrase. The literal form is kept here because Paul is playing on the word: God is ‘King of the ages’, and ‘eternal’ life in verse 16 is from the same root. In Jewish usage ‘eternal life’ is the life of the age to come, a matter of kind as well as of length.

verse.text: This command I commit to you, Timothy, my child, in keeping with the prophecies once made about you, so that with them you may wage the good campaign,

note.term: the prophecies once made about you
note.traditional: the prophecies which went before on thee

verse.note: The Greek can mean prophecies spoken earlier about Timothy, probably at his commissioning (compare 4:14). It can also mean prophecies that ‘led the way to’ him, that is, pointed him out for this work. The first reading is the more common and is followed here.

note.traditional: war a good warfare; fight the good fight

verse.note: The verb and noun are both military, describing a soldier serving on campaign. ‘Fight the good fight’ is better kept for 6:12, where the Greek uses a different image, drawn from athletic contests.

verse.text: holding on to faith and a good conscience. Some have thrust this aside and suffered shipwreck in regard to the faith.
Among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan so that they may be taught not to blaspheme.
verse.note: The same expression appears in 1 Corinthians 5:5 and is generally understood as exclusion from the community, putting the person back into the sphere outside the church where Satan holds sway. The stated purpose is corrective: the verb rendered ‘be taught’ is used of training and disciplining a child. Exactly what the act involved is not known.

verse.text: First of all, then, I urge that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people,
for kings and all who hold high position, so that we may lead a tranquil and quiet life in all godliness and dignity.
verse.note: In the Greek-speaking East the Roman emperor was commonly called by this word, alongside local client kings. A first-century reader would have understood the prayer to include the emperor and his officials.

verse.text: This is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Savior,
who wants all people to be saved and to come to knowledge of the truth.
For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, Christ Jesus, himself human,
verse.note: The Greek uses the same word twice in a row: a mediator between God and 'humans' who is a 'human'. The word means a human being, not specifically a male, and the point is that the mediator shares the nature of those he represents. The traditional 'the man' hides the repetition and can suggest that maleness is in view.

verse.text: who gave himself as a ransom for all, the testimony given at its proper time.

note.term: the testimony given at its proper time
note.traditional: to be testified in due time

verse.note: The Greek is very compressed, literally 'the testimony in its own times', with no verb. It is most often taken to mean that Christ's self-giving was itself God's witness, delivered at the time God chose. Others take it as the testimony now to be proclaimed, which verse 7 then picks up.

verse.text: For this I was appointed a herald and an apostle (I am telling the truth; I am not lying), a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.
verse.note: The Greek word means 'peoples' or 'nations', and in the plural it is the ordinary Jewish term for the non-Jewish peoples. This translation renders the one word as 'Gentiles' or 'nations' according to sense. Here it echoes the 'all people' of verses 1, 4 and 6.

verse.text: So I want the men in every place to pray, lifting up holy hands without anger or argument.
verse.note: Standing with hands raised and palms open was the normal posture of prayer among both Jews and Greeks. The emphasis falls on the character of those praying, not on the gesture.

The word means reasoning or deliberation, and can refer either to inward doubt or to outward dispute. Older versions chose 'doubting'. Most modern translations choose 'quarreling' or 'argument', which pairs more naturally with 'anger'.

verse.text: Likewise, I want women to adorn themselves in respectable dress, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly clothing,
but, as is fitting for women who profess reverence for God, with good works.
A woman should learn in quietness, in all submission.
verse.note: Older versions have 'silence', and the word can mean that. More often it means calm, a settled and undisruptive manner, and its adjective is the 'quiet' life of verse 2 that all believers are to lead. Many modern translations therefore render 'quietness' or 'quietly'. Whether complete silence in the assembly is meant is disputed.

verse.text: I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to be in quietness.
verse.note: The Greek words for 'woman' and 'man' are also the ordinary words for 'wife' and 'husband'. Most interpreters take the general sense here because the surrounding instructions concern the assembly. A minority read verses 11–15 of wife and husband, pointing to the appeal to Adam and Eve and to childbearing.

note.traditional: usurp authority over (KJV); exercise authority over, have authority over (most modern versions)

verse.note: This verb occurs only here in the New Testament and is rare in surviving Greek of the period. It is not the usual word for holding authority. Many scholars take it neutrally, as 'exercise authority'. Others argue for a negative or assertive sense such as 'domineer', 'dictate to' or 'assume authority'. The evidence is too thin to settle the question, and the rendering here follows the majority of modern translations.

verse.text: For Adam was formed first, then Eve;
and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and has come into transgression.
But she will be saved through childbearing, if they remain in faith and love and holiness, with self-control.

note.term: she will be saved through childbearing
note.traditional: she shall be saved in childbearing

verse.note: This is one of the most disputed sentences in the letters. The Greek has 'the childbearing', which some take as the birth of the Messiah, reversing Eve's transgression. Others read 'kept safe through childbirth'. Others again think women will come to salvation in the ordinary course of motherhood and faithful life, not by abandoning it. The verb shifts from 'she' to 'they' without explanation, probably moving from Eve, or woman as a type, to women generally.

verse.text: The saying is trustworthy. If anyone aspires to the position of overseer, it is a good work he desires.

note.traditional: This is a faithful saying / The saying is trustworthy

verse.note: The adjective is normally rendered 'faithful' in this translation, but applied to a statement it means 'reliable, deserving trust', and 'a faithful saying' no longer says that in English. The formula recurs in the letters to Timothy and Titus. It is disputed whether it here endorses what follows about overseers or looks back to the end of chapter 2; the punctuation leaves this open.

The Greek noun means 'oversight', and the related word in verse 2 means 'overseer', a term used for supervisors and officials of many kinds. 'Bishop' derives from this word but now suggests a single leader over many congregations, an arrangement that developed later. Many modern translations also use 'overseer'; others keep 'bishop' for continuity with later usage.

verse.text: So the overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, clear-headed, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach,
verse.note: Literally 'a man of one woman'. The phrase may mean faithful to his wife, married only once (excluding remarriage after death or divorce), or not polygamous; all three have serious defenders. The literal rendering is kept because the Greek does not decide between them. The same phrase recurs in verse 12.

verse.text: not a drunkard, not violent, but gentle, peaceable, not a lover of money,
managing his own household well, keeping his children in submission with all dignity
(but if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's assembly?),
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and, in the Greek Old Testament, for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and is clear enough in reference, but it now suggests a building or institution. This translation uses 'assembly' throughout so that the reader can see it is one word.

verse.text: not a recent convert, so that he does not become conceited and fall into the judgment of the devil.
verse.note: The Greek can mean the judgment that was passed on the devil, which the conceited person would share, or a judgment the devil brings about as accuser. Most interpreters prefer the first. In verse 7 'the snare of the devil' is clearly a snare the devil sets, which leads some to read this verse the same way.

verse.text: He must also have a good reputation with those outside, so that he does not fall into disgrace and the snare of the devil.
Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued, not given to much wine, not greedy for shameful gain,
verse.note: The word is the ordinary Greek term for a servant or someone who carries out a task for another, and is translated 'servant' elsewhere. Here it names a recognised role in the assembly alongside the overseer, so the traditional 'deacon' is kept. The verb 'serve' in verses 10 and 13 is from the same root.

verse.text: holding the mystery of the faith with a clean conscience.
And these too must first be tested; then let them serve, if they are blameless.
Women likewise must be dignified, not slanderers, clear-headed, faithful in everything.
verse.note: The Greek word means both 'woman' and 'wife', and there is no 'their' in the text. The verse may refer to women who serve as deacons or to the wives of deacons; both views are widely held. 'Women' is used because it leaves the question as open as the Greek does.

This is the same Greek word translated 'devil' in verses 6 and 7. As an ordinary adjective it means 'slanderous' or 'given to false accusation'; with the article it had become the standard title for the adversary.

verse.text: Deacons must be husbands of one wife, managing their children and their own households well.
For those who have served well gain a good standing for themselves and great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.
I am writing these things to you, though I hope to come to you soon,
but if I am delayed, so that you may know how one must behave in God's household, which is the assembly of the living God, a pillar and support of the truth.
verse.note: The word can mean a building or the family and dependants who make up a household. It is the same word used in verses 4, 5 and 12 for the households overseers and deacons must manage, and the argument depends on that link, so 'household' is used here too. 'House of God' is the older rendering and may carry an echo of the temple.

verse.text: And beyond dispute, great is the mystery of godliness: He was revealed in flesh, vindicated in spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed in throughout the world, taken up in glory.
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read 'who' (rendered here as 'He'), which begins what is widely thought to be a fragment of an early hymn or confession about Christ. Many later manuscripts read 'God', the basis of the King James rendering 'God was manifest in the flesh'; in ancient script the two readings differ by only a couple of strokes. Nearly all modern editions and translations follow the earlier reading.

The verb is the one translated 'justify' elsewhere, from the same word-family as 'righteousness'; here it means shown or declared to be in the right, probably with reference to the resurrection. The phrase may be 'in spirit', in contrast with 'in flesh' in the previous line, or 'by the Spirit', meaning the Holy Spirit. The Greek allows both and interpreters are divided.

note.traditional: unto the Gentiles / among the nations

verse.note: The Greek plural means both 'nations' and, from a Jewish standpoint, 'Gentiles', the non-Jewish peoples; it is one word. 'Nations' is used here because the parallel line 'in the world' suggests the whole world is in view. 'Among Gentiles' is equally possible and fits Paul's description of himself as a teacher of the Gentiles in 2:7.

verse.text: Now the Spirit says explicitly that in later times some will turn away from the faith, devoting themselves to deceiving spirits and teachings of demons
through the hypocrisy of liars whose own conscience has been seared,
verse.note: The verb means to burn with a hot iron. It may picture a conscience cauterized into numbness, or one branded with a mark of ownership, as slaves and criminals were, here implying ownership by the deceiving powers of verse 1. Most translations and commentators take the first sense, but the second is a serious possibility and cannot be excluded.

verse.text: who forbid marriage and demand abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and have come to know the truth.
For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected when it is received with thanksgiving,
for it is made holy through God’s word and prayer.

note.traditional: the word of God and prayer

verse.note: It is unclear what 'God's word' refers to. It may be God's own declaration in Genesis that what he made is good, or scriptural words spoken in a grace at table, or the gospel message. The translation leaves the phrase as open as the Greek.

verse.text: If you lay these things before the brothers and sisters, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, nourished on the words of the faith and of the good teaching that you have followed closely.
But have nothing to do with profane old wives’ tales. Train yourself instead for godliness;
verse.note: The Greek calls the stories 'profane and old-womanish'. The second word was a stock put-down in philosophical polemic for stories thought unworthy of belief. It is conventional sarcasm aimed at the content of the rival teaching, not a comment on who was spreading it.

verse.text: for training the body is useful for a little, but godliness is useful for everything, holding a promise of life, the present life and the life to come.
verse.note: The Greek phrase can mean 'to a small extent' or 'for a short time'. The contrast with 'for everything' favours extent, but the following mention of the present life and the life to come gives the time sense some support. The rendering keeps the Greek's deliberate parallel between 'a little' and 'everything'.

verse.text: The saying is trustworthy and deserves full acceptance.
verse.note: This translation normally renders the adjective 'faithful' or 'believing'. Here it describes a statement, not a person, and means that the saying can be relied on. 'A faithful saying' is no longer natural English, so 'trustworthy' is used for this formula.

This formula recurs in the letters to Timothy and Titus to mark a statement as established teaching. Here it is disputed whether it points back to the saying about godliness in verse 8 or forward to verse 10. Most interpreters take it as pointing back.

verse.text: For this is why we toil and are reviled: because we have set our hope on the living God, who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe.
verse.note: Manuscripts are divided between 'we are reviled' (the SBLGNT reading, followed here and by the King James tradition) and 'we struggle', which many modern editions and translations prefer. The two Greek words look and sound similar, and either could have given rise to the other.

The usual sense of the word is 'especially', which makes God the Savior of all people and of believers in a particular way. A minority of scholars argue it can mean 'that is to say', which would make 'those who believe' a definition of 'all people'. That sense is disputed, and the ordinary meaning is kept.

verse.text: Command these things and teach them.
Let no one look down on you because you are young, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.
verse.note: In a list of observable qualities the word could equally mean 'faithfulness', that is, reliability. Most translations keep 'faith', and the Greek does not settle the question.

verse.text: Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading, to exhortation, to teaching.
verse.note: The word means reading aloud to a gathering, as the Scriptures were read in the synagogue, not private study. Few people owned books, and most heard the Scriptures only when they were read aloud. The three activities named together look like the elements of a meeting: reading, exhortation based on it, and instruction.

verse.text: Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy, with the laying on of hands by the council of elders.
verse.note: The word names the elders of a community as a body. It is also used of the Jewish council in Jerusalem. Laying on of hands was the recognised gesture for commissioning someone to a task. 2 Timothy 1:6 speaks of Paul's own hands in connection with Timothy's gift, and how the two statements relate is not certain.

verse.text: Practice these things; be absorbed in them, so that your progress may be plain to all.
Keep watch on yourself and on the teaching. Persist in these things, for by doing so you will save both yourself and those who hear you.
Do not speak harshly to an older man, but appeal to him as a father, to younger men as brothers,

note.traditional: an elder (KJV); an older man (most modern versions)

verse.note: The Greek word means both an older man and an elder who holds office in the community. Here it is paired with younger men, older women and younger women, so age is meant. In verses 17 and 19 the same word refers to the office and is rendered 'elder'.

verse.text: to older women as mothers, to younger women as sisters, in all purity.
Honor widows who are truly widows.
verse.note: In this passage 'honor' includes material support, not only respect. The following verses concern who should provide for widows, and the related noun in verse 17 is connected with a worker's wages. The word echoes the commandment to honor father and mother, which was understood to include caring for them in old age.

verse.text: But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn to show devotion to their own household and to repay their parents and grandparents, for this is acceptable before God.
verse.note: The verb describes fulfilling one's sacred duty, and was used of dutiful conduct toward parents and family as well as toward the gods. 'Godliness' now suggests private religious feeling, whereas the point here is a religious obligation discharged by caring for one's own family.

verse.text: The one who is truly a widow, left all alone, has set her hope on God and continues in petitions and prayers night and day;
but the one who lives for pleasure is dead while she lives.
Command these things as well, so that they may be above reproach.
But if anyone does not provide for their own people, and especially for members of their household, they have denied the faith and are worse than an unbeliever.
Let a widow be enrolled if she is not less than sixty years old, the wife of one husband,

note.traditional: be enrolled / be put on the list

verse.note: The verb means to enter someone on an official list. The community evidently kept a register of widows. It is debated whether this was simply a list of those entitled to support or a recognised group who also had duties of prayer and service; verses 11–12 suggest that enrollment involved some kind of commitment.

Literally 'a woman of one man'. It may mean she was married only once, an ideal praised in ancient epitaphs, or that she was faithful to her husband during the marriage. Since verse 14 urges younger widows to remarry, many interpreters prefer the second reading, but the question is not settled.

verse.text: well attested for good works: if she has raised children, if she has shown hospitality to strangers, if she has washed the feet of holy ones, if she has helped those in distress, if she has devoted herself to every good work.
verse.note: The word refers to all members of the believing community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. 'Saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue, which is not meant here. Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people'.

verse.text: But decline younger widows; for when their desires draw them away from Christ, they want to marry,

note.term: their desires draw them away from Christ
note.traditional: wax wanton against Christ / their passions draw them away from Christ

verse.note: The verb occurs only here in the New Testament and is very rare elsewhere. The simpler related verb means to live in sensual indulgence, and the compound adds the idea of doing so against someone. The sense appears to be that strong desires, probably sexual, set them at odds with their commitment to Christ; the precise nuance is uncertain.

verse.text: and so they incur judgment, because they have set aside their first pledge.
verse.note: The word usually rendered 'faith' also meant a pledge or solemn promise, and with the verb used here ('set aside, annul') it formed a recognised idiom for breaking one's word. The reference is probably to a commitment made on enrollment, perhaps to remain unmarried in Christ's service. The traditional rendering 'their first faith' is possible, but it would imply that remarriage is itself an abandonment of the faith, which verse 14 contradicts.

verse.text: At the same time they also learn to be idle, going around from house to house, and not only idle but also gossips and busybodies, saying things they should not.
So I want the younger ones to marry, bear children, manage their households, and give the adversary no opening for abuse.
For some have already turned aside to follow Satan.
If any believing woman has widows in her family, let her help them, and let the assembly not be burdened, so that it can help those who are truly widows.

note.traditional: any man or woman that believeth (KJV)

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read 'any believing woman'. Many later manuscripts read 'any believing man or woman', and that longer form lies behind the King James Version. It is generally thought that scribes expanded the text because it seemed odd to limit the duty to women. The shorter reading is followed here.

The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint's word for Israel assembled. 'Church' now suggests a building or an institution, so this translation uses 'assembly' throughout. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering, and readers will recognise that the same community is meant.

verse.text: Let the elders who lead well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching;
verse.note: The Greek word means both honor and a price or payment, and could be used of an honorarium. The quotations about the ox and the worker's wages in the next verse show that material support is at least included. Whether 'double' means twice the pay of others, or respect together with pay, or simply generous provision, is disputed.

verse.text: for the Scripture says, “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing,” and, “The worker is worthy of his wages.”

note.term: “The worker is worthy of his wages.”
note.traditional: The labourer is worthy of his reward / deserves his wages

verse.note: The first quotation is Deuteronomy 25:4. The second is not found in the Jewish Scriptures; it matches word for word a saying of Jesus in Luke 10:7. Whether the author cites a written Gospel as Scripture, or the phrase 'the Scripture says' strictly covers only the first quotation with a well-known saying added, is debated.

verse.text: Do not accept an accusation against an elder unless it rests on two or three witnesses.
Those who persist in sinning, reprove in front of everyone, so that the rest also may be afraid.
I solemnly charge you before God and Christ Jesus and the chosen angels to keep these things without prejudgment, doing nothing out of partiality.
Do not be quick to lay hands on anyone, and do not share in the sins of others; keep yourself pure.
verse.note: Laying on of hands was the gesture by which someone was commissioned for a role in the community (see 4:14). In this context about elders, the warning is most likely against appointing someone to office too hastily and so sharing responsibility for that person's later failings. A minority view takes it as the readmission of a disciplined offender.

verse.text: Stop drinking only water, and use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses.
The sins of some people are plain to see, going ahead of them to judgment; but those of others follow after them.
In the same way good works too are plain to see, and even those that are not cannot stay hidden.
All who are under the yoke as slaves must regard their own masters as worthy of all honor, so that the name of God and the teaching may not be slandered.

Those whose masters are believers must not look down on them because they are brothers; rather, they must serve them all the more, because those who benefit from their good service are believers and beloved. Teach these things and urge them.

note.term: those who benefit from their good service
note.traditional: those who benefit by their good service

verse.note: The Greek is literally 'those who take hold of the good deed'. Most interpreters take this as the masters who receive the slaves' service, which strikingly casts the slave as the benefactor. The phrase can also mean 'those who devote themselves to doing good', describing the masters as benefactors; the grammar allows either.

verse.text: If anyone teaches otherwise and does not hold to healthy words, those of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the teaching that accords with godliness,
verse.note: The traditional 'sound' hides a medical metaphor. The Greek word means 'to be in good health', and the next verse sets it against a teacher who is 'sick' with a craving for disputes. 'Healthy' keeps the contrast the author built.

verse.text: he is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing, but is sick with a craving for disputes and battles over words. From these come envy, strife, slander, evil suspicions,
and constant wrangling among people corrupted in mind and deprived of the truth, who suppose that godliness is a way to profit.
Godliness with contentment is in fact a way to great profit;
verse.note: The word was a favourite of Stoic and Cynic philosophers, for whom it meant self-sufficiency: needing nothing beyond what one has. Here it is given a religious setting, and the related verb appears in verse 8 ('we will be content'). The same Greek word for 'a way to profit' is used in verses 5 and 6, so the author is turning the opponents' own claim back on them.

verse.text: for we brought nothing into the world, and neither can we carry anything out of it;

note.traditional: and we cannot take anything out

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts join the two clauses with a word that normally means 'because' or 'that', which is awkward here. Later copyists smoothed it by adding 'it is clear that' or 'it is true that'. Most translations, like this one, treat the connection as loose; some take it as 'so that' or 'just as'.

verse.text: but if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content.
But those who want to be rich fall into temptation and a snare and many senseless and harmful desires, which plunge people into ruin and destruction;
for the love of money is the root of all evils, and some, in reaching for it, have been led astray from the faith and have pierced themselves with many pains.

note.traditional: a root of all kinds of evil

verse.note: The Greek has no article before 'root', so it can be read as 'a root' or 'the root'; a predicate noun placed before the verb often lacks the article even when definite. The following phrase is plainly 'all evils', which most modern versions soften to 'all kinds of evil'. The sentence has the form of a proverb, and Greek moralists had similar sayings; such maxims state things absolutely without claiming there are no exceptions.

verse.text: But you, O man of God, flee these things, and pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance, gentleness.
Contend in the good contest of the faith; take hold of the eternal life to which you were called, and for which you made the good confession in the presence of many witnesses.
verse.note: The noun and its verb ordinarily refer to an athletic contest, such as a race or a wrestling or boxing match, and by extension to any strenuous struggle. 'Fight the good fight' suggests warfare to a modern reader, which is not the usual picture. 'Contend' and 'contest' also preserve the Greek's repetition of one word-family.

The adjective is formed from the word for 'age'. In Jewish usage 'eternal life' is the life of the age to come, different in kind as well as unending. The chapter plays on this: the rich are rich 'in the present age' (verse 17) and are urged to take hold of 'the life that is truly life' (verse 19).

verse.text: I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who in his witness before Pontius Pilate made the good confession,
verse.note: The preposition can mean 'in the presence of', as of someone appearing before a magistrate, or 'in the time of'. The first is chosen because it parallels Timothy's own confession 'in the presence of many witnesses'. On the second reading the phrase would refer to Jesus' whole witness, including his death, under Pilate's governorship.

verse.text: to keep the commandment spotless and beyond reproach until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ,
which the blessed and only Sovereign will display in its own time—the King of those who reign as kings and Lord of those who rule as lords,

note.term: the King of those who reign as kings and Lord of those who rule as lords
note.traditional: the King of kings and Lord of lords

verse.note: The Greek here does not use the nouns 'kings' and 'lords', as Revelation does, but participles: those who are reigning and those who are ruling. The traditional wording assimilates this verse to the more familiar title. The meaning is much the same, with the emphasis on those who currently hold power.

verse.text: who alone has immortality, who dwells in unapproachable light, whom no human being has seen or can see. To him be honor and eternal might. Amen.
Charge those who are rich in the present age not to be haughty, nor to set their hope on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything for our enjoyment;
they are to do good, to be rich in good works, to be generous and ready to share,
storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the life that is truly life.
O Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you, turning away from the profane empty talk and contradictions of what is falsely called knowledge,

note.term: what has been entrusted to you
note.traditional: that which is committed to thy trust; the deposit

verse.note: The word is a legal and commercial term for property left in another person's keeping, which the keeper was bound to return intact. Here it stands for the teaching Timothy has received and must preserve unaltered.

The opponents evidently claimed a special 'knowledge' (Greek gnosis). The word later gave its name to the movements called Gnostic, but the letter does not give enough detail to identify these teachers with any known later system, and scholars disagree about how far the connection goes. 'Contradictions' may mean their counter-arguments or the self-contradictions of their teaching.

verse.text: which some have professed and so have missed the mark regarding the faith. Grace be with you.
verse.note: The 'you' is plural in the earliest manuscripts, so a letter addressed to one person closes with a blessing on a wider group, presumably the congregation that would hear it read. Many later manuscripts have the singular, and some add 'Amen'.
